title: Best Golf Rangefinders UK
short: Eleven laser rangefinders tested over multiple rounds, from a budget model with slope to GPS hybrids and ultra-compact lasers.
intro: A rangefinder's real test is how quickly and reliably it locks onto the flag among trees and bushes, round after round. This guide compares rangefinders tested by Golf Monthly's Conor Keenan, who heads up their rangefinder, GPS and golf watch reviews, with help from colleagues. They test on-course over multiple rounds and in different conditions. The source lists a Nikon Coolshot heading over a Voice Caddie write-up, so the Voice Caddie entry here follows the text and specification table.

products.name: Tour Hybrid
products.best_for: Golfers who want laser accuracy plus instant GPS yardages to the green in one device
products.key_spec: Built-in GPS front, centre and back yardages in the viewfinder, slope-compensated, 6x, 1,300 yards, IPX6
products.summary: Golf Monthly's top pick and the best Bushnell they've tested: as you lock onto the pin, GPS front, centre and back distances to the green appear in the viewfinder. Its GPS activates instantly with no third-party apps or manual course selection, and slope-compensated distances work on both laser and GPS readings, though the viewfinder graphics could be a touch clearer.
pros: Built-in GPS gives a more accurate picture of your approach shot
GPS picks up the course quickly and automatically
Slope-compensated distances on both laser and GPS
cons: Graphics through the viewfinder could be a touch clearer

products.name: Golf 900 Laser Rangefinder
products.best_for: Golfers who want accurate yardages and slope at a low price
products.key_spec: 5-1,300 yards (flag 350), 6x, slope switch, First Target Priority, IPX2, 5,000 measurements
products.summary: Golf Monthly found this performed valiantly against the Bushnell Tour V5 Shift, with a clear 6x view and a sturdy feel that held up in strong conditions. A First Target Priority system picks out the flagstick from trees and bushes and confirms with a vibration, accuracy stayed within +/- 1 yard, and slope compensation is rarely seen this cheaply, though it lacks the premium look of others.
pros: Slope functionality that can be easily disabled
cons: Lacks the premium appeal of others visually

products.name: Pro L5
products.best_for: Golfers who want a clear OLED display and a stylish white finish without overspending
products.key_spec: Ultra-clear OLED display, 7x, 1,300 yards, cart magnet, about 5,800 measurements
products.summary: Golf Monthly says this marks a turning point for Shot Scope, addressing feedback on earlier models with its first ultra-clear OLED display. The display is bright and clear, it's easy to pick the flag out of a busy background, and a magnet mounts it on a cart, but it lacks a premium look and feel.
pros: Easy to pick out the flag from a busy background
Magnet for mounting on a cart
cons: Lacks a premium look and feel

products.name: Tour V7 Shift
products.best_for: Golfers who want a class-leading OLED viewfinder and fast, reliable yardages
products.key_spec: OLED display showing standard yardage in orange and slope-adjusted in green, 6x, 1,300 yards, IPX6, USB-C
products.summary: Golf Monthly found the V7 builds on the popular V6 with thoughtful improvements, including a brilliant OLED display, a premium metal-detailed waterproof build and Pinseeker with Visual Jolt confirmation of a pin lock. It also adds a yardage recall button and Foresight Sports club recommendations, though many of its unique features aren't legal for competition use.
cons: Many of the unique features aren't legal for competition use

products.name: Captain Pro
products.best_for: Golfers who want smart features and GPS via an app at a mid-tier price
products.key_spec: 7x OLED display, flag-lock vibration, IP67, USB-C, app with GPS yardages and club recommendations, 1,200 yards
products.summary: Golf Monthly found features you'd expect on a device costing more than double, wrapped in a tough IP67 dust and waterproof rubber body with a crystal-clear 7x OLED display. Paired with the Blue Tees app it gives front, centre and back GPS yardages, aerial hole views and green heat maps, with an analytics subscription unlocking shot tracking, though the app could be improved.
pros: Part of the growing, affordable Blue Tees ecosystem
cons: Carry case could do with an elastic clip

products.name: Titan Elite Laser Rangefinder
products.best_for: Golfers who want a tough, feature-packed laser with a lost-device finder
products.key_spec: Premium aluminium shell, IP67, 6x, 999 yards, USB-C, Find My Precision Pro, MySlope sync
products.summary: Golf Monthly recommends this for anyone wanting a more durable laser than average, with a Visual Target Lock giving a lag-free pulse and ripple on the reticle so you know you've hit the flag rather than trees behind the green. Slope mode can sync with MySlope to your ball flight, the app connection is among the simplest they've tried, and Find My Precision Pro helps locate a dropped device.
pros: Switching in and out of GPS mode is very easy
cons: Could have a slightly more premium aesthetic
products.search: Precision Pro Titan Elite laser rangefinder

products.name: GenePro G1
products.best_for: Data-driven golfers who like a laser and a GPS map in one device
products.key_spec: 6x laser plus 2.13in AMOLED GPS touchscreen, 43,000+ preloaded courses, IPX7, about 15 hours
products.summary: Golf Monthly found a unique hybrid combining a high-performing laser with a built-in touchscreen GPS showing green layouts, hazards and layup distances, plus flag-lock pulse and a rotating ring to toggle slope. The screen is vibrant and the laser fast, but the touchscreen can feel laggy and the GPS doesn't always automatically change holes on the next tee.
pros: A lot of product for the money
cons: GPS doesn't always automatically change holes on the next tee

products.name: Laser Fit 2
products.best_for: Golfers who want an ultra-compact, pocket-sized laser
products.key_spec: Under four ounces, 7x, 1,000 yards, Pin Tracer target lock, Ball-to-Pin triangulation, about 70 rounds
products.summary: Golf Monthly found a very compact, pocket-sized laser for golfers who prioritise speed and portability, with rapid readouts from Pin Tracer target locking and a Ball-to-Pin triangulation mode for measuring from a cart on cart-path-only days. Interchangeable accent rings personalise it, but the outer casing is somewhat plasticky and, surprisingly, no carrying case is included.
pros: Rapid readings with Pin Tracer target lock

products.name: A1-Slope
products.best_for: Golfers who want a small, sturdy laser with slope and long battery life
products.key_spec: 350+ yards, 6x, IPX6, slope switch, JOLT vibrations, BITE magnetic cart mount, 12+ hours
products.summary: Bushnell's smallest rangefinder in the current lineup, which Golf Monthly found sturdy and well built, with fast, accurate readings with slope on or off. JOLT vibrations reliably confirm a flag lock, it has a magnetic cart mount and exceptional battery life, though the display could be clearer, particularly when shrubbery sits behind the green.
pros: Excellent accuracy, especially the slope feature
cons: Graphics on the display could have stood out more

products.name: Pro X3+
products.best_for: Golfers who want the most accurate yardages and don't mind the price and weight
products.key_spec: 7x, 600+ yards, IPX7, factors in slope, temperature and barometric pressure, Bluetooth app, wind data
products.summary: Golf Monthly says that if price were no object this would likely be its top pick, setting the standard for how good a rangefinder can be by factoring in distance, slope, temperature and elevation. It's waterproof with a solid weight that helps golfers with shaky hands, and pairs with the Bushnell Golf app, though the new wind feature was a faff to calibrate and it feels heavy.
pros: Partnering app enhances ease of use

products.name: Pro X
products.best_for: Golfers who want a reasonably priced laser with a personalised look
products.key_spec: Slope on/off for competition, 6x, 800 yards, built-in cart magnet, target lock vibration, about 5,800 measures
products.summary: Golf Monthly found a reasonably priced rangefinder that appeals to a wide range of players, with slope-adjusted distances that turn off easily for competition, target lock vibration and a built-in cart magnet. It stands out for customisable designs, from stock graphics and country flags to custom logos, and works with the app for aerial GPS maps, but the viewfinder is slightly dim.
pros: Works alongside the app to give aerial GPS maps
cons: A little dull down the viewfinder

guide.q: Laser rangefinder or GPS: which do I need?
guide.a: A laser gives an exact distance to whatever you aim at, such as the flag, but needs line of sight. GPS gives distances to the front, middle and back of the green and hazards without aiming. Hybrids like the Bushnell Tour Hybrid and Mileseey GenePro G1 here combine both, so you don't have to choose.

guide.q: Is slope useful, and is it legal?
guide.a: Slope-adjusted distance accounts for elevation change, which can change which club you need. Most rangefinders here let you switch slope off, as the Inesis 900 and Shot Scope Pro X do, because slope isn't allowed in competitions, and Golf Monthly notes many of the Bushnell Tour V7 Shift's extra features aren't legal for competition use.

guide.q: Why does pin lock vibration matter?
guide.a: It confirms you've locked onto the flag and not trees or bushes behind the green, a problem that has plagued many rangefinders. The Inesis 900, Bushnell A1-Slope and Bushnell Tour V7 Shift here all give a vibration or pulse when the pin is locked.

guide.q: How much do I need to spend?
guide.a: Less than you might think: Golf Monthly found budget rangefinders like the Inesis 900 now deliver accurate yardages and slope, so basic models are no longer a waste of money. Spending more buys features such as a brighter OLED display, GPS, app integration and durability, as on the Blue Tees Captain Pro, Bushnell Tour Hybrid and Precision Pro Titan Elite.
